body.text: in brief
• Health authorities worry Russia could be concealing a deadly Siberian lab leak.
• Experts warn weak global oversight leaves the world vulnerable to outbreaks.

Health authorities are becoming increasingly concerned Russia is concealing information about a potentially serious pathogenic outbreak, following the death of a plague lab technician and the quarantining of dozens of people.
The incident has caught global attention, despite the lack of clear information coming out of Russia, and highlighted serious problems with global efforts to monitor disease labs.

Leading disease outbreak expert Professor Raina MacIntyre of the Kirby Institute told SBS News that the incident highlights just how exposed the world is to pathogenic threat in an era of fracturing global governance institutions.

"The US and a couple of other countries have left the WHO [World Health Organization], so the WHO is no longer a global organisation," she said. "It's got limited remit, and it's got no regulatory or legislative power."
"We just have to look at COVID and what happened there."
Both the United States and the WHO have called for transparency about the incident in Russia's central-eastern Siberian region last week.
WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said clear communication is "essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks".
Local media and health authorities have reported that five hospitals, the research lab, and around 200 close contacts of the deceased technician had been put under lockdown or restrictions.

Russia's health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor has since said that the cause of death of 28-year-old Darya Shipilova was not plague but "pneumonia of undetermined etiology" and that no further cases have been identified. Some local media reports and government statements claiming the incident was plague-related have since been altered or removed.
US President Donald Trump has said he will speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin directly about the incident and has previously offered to send medical help.

The US State Department has said it is "watching closely". The Wall Street Journal has reported that it sent Russia a confidential communication warning that failure to disclose details of the incident runs against its international health responsibilities.

Four neighbouring nations, including Kazakhstan and Mongolia, have introduced heightened health screenings at border crossings; however, the WHO maintains that the risk to the international community remains "very low".

MacIntyre said that while it is too early to determine the nature of the incident, Russia's shifting narrative and rapid response has her concerned since pathogenic lab leaks often prompt similar responses from governments.
"There's generally pretty much always cover-up, denial, obfuscation of facts, and long, long delays before anyone finds out what really went on," she said.

"The incubation period of plague is quite short, usually no longer than seven days. So if we see people continuing to be quarantined into next week and the week after, then we know something really serious is going on."
Concerns of a Russian cover-up

Shipilova worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia. She is reported to have become ill in late September, and was admitted to hospital in the neighbouring town of Shelekhov on 29 September with severe respiratory symptoms. She died on 1 or 2 October.

Local independent Russian media outlet People of Baikal reported that she contracted pneumonic plague after accidentally breaking a test tube containing the bacteria Yersinia pestis while at work. Alternative reports claim that she contracted the virus after a recent work trip near the Mongolian border.

Dr Thomas Jeffries, senior lecturer in microbiology at Western Sydney University, told SBS News that the bacteria in question is the same one responsible for the Black Death — which "wiped out" around half of the European population in the 14th century — and is expressed in three different forms; bubonic, pneumonic, and septicemic.

Plague bacteria remains present in wild rodents and their fleas across much of the world, with an estimated 1,000 to 2,000 cases per year and 50 to 100 deaths. Mongolia, western China, Kazakhstan, and south-eastern Russia are known hotspots.
Jeffries said that while Shipilova may have contracted the disease from an animal, a lab leak "seems like a reasonable possibility", though he urges caution.
"The main link with plague is that the lady that died is from a plague research institute and ... the symptoms are in line with it being the plague," he said.
"But there's no released information of an actual laboratory test confirming that it's the plague."
He said while antibiotics do "cure" the plague, they need to be administered "pretty early".
"Whether there was a delay in her getting the antibiotics, whether it's a different pathogen altogether — that information doesn't exist," Jeffries said.
Irkutsk regional governor Igor Kobzev has said Rospotrebnadzor has determined that "no microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples".

There have been "no new cases of staff from the anti-plague institute seeking medical attention" since Shipilova's death, he added, saying that the health situation in the region "remains under our control and that of the experts".

However, Jeffries said that the "political situation in Russia" — a country which frequently places near the bottom of democratic and press freedom rankings — makes reliable information hard to discern and that the WHO is really "the source of information we should be relying on".
Lab leaks and 'dual-function' research

While the incident in Russia remains difficult to determine, MacIntyre said that potentially dangerous biological research is constantly being carried out across the globe and that lab leaks are "quite common".

EpiWatch — a global biosecurity monitoring and detection program headed by MacIntyre at the University of New South Wales — believes there are around 3,000 biosafety level 3 and 4 labs (the two highest levels) conducting high-consequence work around the world.

Many of these are likely conducting "dual-function" work — research which could be used to help or harm humanity — but MacIntyre said that, as there is "no global register or data" on that, there is simply "no way of knowing" the number of research facilities or what they are studying.

"Looking at lab leaks from the year 2000 till 2024, there were hundreds," she said. "Sometimes they resulted in human infections, sometimes they resulted in outbreaks, sometimes they resulted in people dying of those infections."

In 1979, a technician working at a secret biological weapons research and production facility in the Russian city of Yekaterinburg forgot to alert his colleagues that he had removed an air filter in the lab. As a result, aerosolised anthrax was pumped into the surrounding environment for hours, killing dozens of people.

Russia claimed the outbreak was natural and the US team sent to investigate agreed, something MacIntyre said shows that global institutions are "at the mercy" of nations sharing information accurately.
MacIntyre quoted 2015 research which found that "the risk of an unnatural pandemic — either from a lab leak or a deliberate event — was much higher than that of a natural pandemic".
"That is even more so the case today," she said.

The Biological Weapons Convention, the primary agreement governing bio-weapon research and manufacture, came into force in 1975. Jeffries cautions that the expansion of dual-function research globally demands an update to the convention. However, he also believes its eventual value will be determined by the people who use it.
"Like any technology, it's just going to reflect human nature," he said.
"We split the atom, and you can either use that for nuclear power, or you can make a bomb."
